comments.content:
Well—wait. Is it not well known that the end-game for Astro is almost certainly to sell the company?

They’ve taken $10M from investors—likely to result in the same funding problem that Gatsby had—except with (imo) an even larger risk as they don’t seem to have started monetization efforts.

Certainly not claiming that Eleventy’s problems or risks are better, just different.

We’ve taken $0 from investors, which is definitely easier for me to manage long-term (what I’m optimizing for).

@zachleat In my experience, 95% of all VC funded competitors in our areas will vanish when you are playing the long-term game and just wait long enough. The other 5% will become so expensive that they end up as enterprise systems for a very exclusive audience.

@zachleat

I guess I'm old school, but it twists my brain into a knot trying to understand the ecosystem around venture funded open source projects.

It's so counter to ... everything I've known about software up until 2019.

I guess, 20 years into the future, we'll see this as a strange blip.
@kixxauth would you call it a zero interest rate phenomenon

@zachleat I think “more well understood” would be fair. It’s an open source framework with an MIT license.

I assume you own some domain names and graphics and such, and otherwise it can be endlessly remixed for people to try alternate paths.

The hard work of maintenance and compatibility, never mind new features, docs, community management, gets done as much as people volunteer or are paid to do it.
@zachleat Maybe I'm out of the loop but I'd also like to know how they want to earn money, the initial post didn’t say https://astro.build/blog/the-astro-technology-company/

@boris I think the same could be said of Astro too, no? The framework is also open source/open licensed.

The nuance I’ve been thinking about is more FTE => biting off larger problems => larger code base => more maintenance risk when the company is sold.

Just for comparison I don’t think volunteers will maintain Gatsby given that the framework is owned by Netlify (and Netlify is laying off folks that used to do the job of maintaining Gatsby)

@zachleat Ha! Yeah, I guess from a capital and finance perspective it is very reflective of a zero interest rate era :D

Never would have guessed it would impact open source web development frameworks ;-p
@lekoarts I haven’t heard anything about it either, fwiw
@bastianallgeier whew!

@zachleat that is 100% why I will not use it. Because it is not upfront with how they intend to monetise.

It is so clear that they are intending to sell it to someone else. This feels extremely sour to me, because especially with these types of technologies, you are selling a community, or access to a community.

I didn't say anything because I thought I was just paranoid, but that is just how venture capitalism works, and they very much participate.

No shade to the devs, but it is a reality.

@zachleat yikes... just.. yikes.

What was all that projected competing with next.js for then? Obviously not to make a better product, but to appeal as a competitor so that they can get bought.
@zachleat @kixxauth lol good one! :D
@zachleat @kixxauth deep lore meme

@zachleat yes the attendant dedicated entity with funding makes it muddier. For GPL (for instance), having an entity hold all the copyrights gives only it the ability to re-license.

Now that we know they won’t pursue hosting, what larger codebase features and thus services might they offer.

Potentially parallels Gatsby -> Gatsby Cloud entanglement.

Something something “maintainer deficit”

@kixxauth I can very much recommend this episode from Tech Won't Save Us: https://techwontsave.us/episode/180_abolish_venture_capital_w_edward_ongweso_jr

TLDR; Venture Capital is a plague on society that keeps on festering and intends to infiltrate all parts of human living, to commodify the most mundane parts of it.
@boris ah just for the record I don’t think this *changes* their stance on whether or not they will pursue hosting—previously Netlify was the official hosting partner.

@nachtfunke ah, hmm—I don’t think I see it like that.

Vercel needs to diversify beyond Next.js long-term. And every framework (including Astro) is naturally competing for Next.js’ marketshare.

Vercel made a very smart move to diversify with Svelte. This is another example of that.

@zachleat But to customers, it means that all products, as in services, eventually are planned to be considered obsolete or at least not profitable, is that not so?

I see why that makes sense for Vercel, but why would I convert to a customer, when the reason for why they take up this product into their portfolio is because they know the product will eventually become obsolete?

Maybe I see this way to pessimistic, but I have yet to see a business operation of this nature that is good for people

@nachtfunke oh, well—this is money for Astro—partnerships aren’t bad! I don’t think Vercel wants Astro to fail or become obsolete because of Next.js bias. They want a diversified portfolio of successful things.

The framework’s sustainability risk would increase dramatically when Astro sells—but this partnership is unlikely to change the equation of that much.

@zachleat for sure, it just means that there’s a blank space that isn’t hosting where we need to imagine paid services.

Having already switched official partners, we know that hosting isn’t tightly coupled in the open source framework.
@zachleat This is exactly why I ditched any interest in it the moment VC funding was announced.

@zachleat oh no. It's my fav problematic?

...Got any guides on porting an astro project (I don't use any other big libraries or frameworks within it) to 11ty...?
@sarajw ah—I certainly didn’t mean to suggest that it was problematic?
@zachleat well the following conversation makes it sound like it might get tricky to use at some point, for free anyway 🫠

@sarajw ah, hmm—I don’t think they’ll bait and switch to a pay-for-use model. I’d imagine that the framework will continue to exist to use for free.

The nuance here is that when a company around a framework sells, the risk around whether or not that framework will continue to be maintained goes up quite a bit!
@sarajw conversely, frameworks that aren’t VC-funded have risks too (see https://fediverse.zachleat.com/@zachleat/110968012104388814)
@zachleat Dang, well, guess I might be moving my hastily ported personal site from Astro to…something else
@jkohlmann I don’t think I’d recommend that—port when porting is needed, I think!

@zachleat Touché 🙇🏼‍♂️ I chose Astro since it made it easy to incrementally move my old PHP and Sass site to something a bit more modern. In my case, that also means, if I ever do anything more with it, it’ll be a more elaborate rewrite. Thus I’d consider switching libraries / static site generators.
@zachleat ok that all makes more sense, thank you :)
@zachleat
@zachleat Wonder what happens if / when Vercel run out of money…

@zachleat everybody wants to crack the WordPress hegemony. They just haven’t found the right combination of frontend/backend/cms yet.

No monetization strategy we know of is a bad look for Astro. Sad, because their community and contributors are great. Their Discord is super lively but moderated really well and very helpful. Their docs are super helpful and thorough.
@flori yeah, well said—the whole team is awesome
@andydavies @zachleat *Both* of them are giant stacks of VC money with no exit strategy.
@zachleat We'll see about that 🤷🤷
@lekoarts @zachleat We don't 💪
@eliancodes @lekoarts I think the concern here is that folks are worried that a VC-backed company without a monetization strategy is a pretty risky thing to bet on

@andydavies @zachleat And what happens? They both keep gobbling up little companies (despite Netlify once promising to want a healthy ecosystem) in a weird egg-and-spoon race until either one of the 4 companies that can afford them buys one, because I can’t see either hitting IPO. Their margins are too thin (and I doubt either is revenue+, or even close). So we’ll get one as a sub brand of something you already know, and the other gets an acqui-hire out or something.
@phae @zachleat Yeh, can’t see how they’d be profitable on $50mn / yr revenue

@matthewp @zachleat @eliancodes For my hobby projects I wouldn’t care, for my business I would care a lot.

Bit surprised to hear that there are no concrete plans, normally no one just gives money away for free.

Projects like Next, Astro, Gatsby, etc. are so complex, once no one gets paid anymore to work on them it’s impossible for the community to immediately pick it up unless preparations were made and non-company core contributors were taught.

@zachleat I’ve lamented similar previously too (https://twitter.com/benschwarz/status/1585482090971136001). Gatsby’s seed was $5m at a time when that was described by some as a “mango” seed round (yes, I know 🤮).

It sounds weird, but you can raise a bunch of money to get 3-5 years down the line, then side step to actual adults take over when it’s probably too late anyway. Tech never learns.
@andydavies @phae @zachleat they’ve raised over $300M, even with their fairly significant headcount there’s a while to go

@zachleat Eleventy is for sure more of a community project than these VC infused projects.

One reason I eg have staid away from Prisma, Rome, Deno and similar.

When the VC money runs out there will be no one left to maintain them.

And VC:s sacrifices most companies in the hunt for the truly massive ones, so it’s always more likely that a VC-funded startup will fail than that it will succeed.
@jkohlmann @zachleat have you thought about porting it to PHP
@developit @zachleat I mean…I’d consider it, tbh (for this kind of site, anyway)
@developit @jkohlmann @zachleat hey there is nothing wrong with PHP! (Says the person who works with the dude who wrote PHP)
@ksylor @jkohlmann @zachleat lol oh I agree, was a genuine suggestion :P
@ksylor @developit @zachleat Legitimately “the best kind of static site generator is no static site generator”
@developit @ksylor @zachleat Yeah, I took it as such, don’t worry

@jkohlmann @ksylor @zachleat

function* generator() {
yield 'static site'
}
@developit @ksylor @zachleat Dang, all this time, I could’ve gone frameworkless
@jkohlmann @ksylor @developit objection!!! Permission to treat as a hostile witness 😅
@sarajw @zachleat We still haven't found an ideal sustainable business model for giving a product/service away for free. Everything is trade-offs.

@AmeliaBR @zachleat yeah, that's true. And I'm slowly adapting to the idea of paying for stuff again, hahah.

Once you get used to using lots of different things at a low level it's so hard to choose who to pay and stick with.

@zachleat Right, both options have risks. I think many framework authors moved in the funded direction because of the risks of being independent (i.e. minimal funding combined with high demand for resources). Funding solves the resources issue, but adds the risk of return on investment (i.e. monetize, get bought or go out of business). I'm obviously not saying anything you don't know, but, point is, the risk from an end user's perspective is probably similar (the project is no longer maintained)

@zachleat The problem for end-users right now is there are few alternatives. Eleventy is independent, but Next/Svelte are under Vercel (I know the structure is different), Gatsby is Netlify, Astro is VC funded. Essentially these all come with "preferred vendors" whether it's acknowledged or not. Not that end users are innocent in the equation. The demands we've put on framework authors have, in my opinion, almost forced them to seek funding.
@zachleat I know about the $16B Zach. Pepperidge farm remembers.

@sarajw @zachleat And of course, the flipside is: with so many free options for software, there's no guarantee that a paid option will get a big enough customer base to be economically sustainable, either.

@remotesynth @zachleat If I’m correct, Vercel owns and maintains Next, but Svelte is “owned” 100% by @rich_harris.

Vue/Nuxt are not “belonging” to any other corpo.

@AmeliaBR
And it's not just software - I have the same problem with newspapers...

@zachleat

@meduz @zachleat @rich_harris I noted that the structure of Svelte under Vercel is different. As I understand it, Rich is paid full time by Vercel to work on it but it isn't owned by Vercel. And, yes, Vue is afaik funded through sponsorships.
@ben_seven the @davatron5000 check never cleared!!!
@zachleat @davatron5000 rogue banking error, surely he’s good for it

@remotesynth Yeah, this all seems accurate to me. The one weird piece is that the risk to authors is fairly well known (to authors) but the risk to app developers (end users/framework consumers) is not.
@AmeliaBR @sarajw the awkward variable here is that VC-funding often has much higher minimums for success than *mere* profitability
@zachleat @AmeliaBR Yeah. ROI can do one.

@sarajw @zachleat I've seen analyses that suggest many VCs would rather have a company they invested go bankrupt (so they could get a tax write-off against other sources of income) rather than have it be barely profitable.
@AmeliaBR @zachleat oh, that's sad.
@benschwarz @phae @zachleat Guess how long that lasts depends on the gap between their income and expenditure
